fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, actually. Right now the picture is pretty fragmented. Every lab trains a big base model, then does its own post-training, and if they want the model to know about something new they either retrain from scratch or do some fine-tuning internally. And from the outside, you basically get a snapshot. The model is frozen at some point in time, and the knowledge is frozen with it.

What I'd really like to see is something closer to how we develop software. Think about how an open source codebase evolves. Nobody rebuilds the whole thing every time there's a new feature. People contribute patches, there's a review process, there's versioning, and the project moves forward incrementally. I'd love for the model itself to become more like that kind of living artifact, where updates to the model are something the community can contribute to, not just the lab that trained it.

Concretely, that means a few things. One, we need to understand continual training much better than we do today. Right now if you keep training a model on new data, you run into forgetting, you run into drift, and we don't have very principled tools for deciding what to keep and what to overwrite. A lot of the current practice is heuristics, like mixing in replay data and hoping it's fine. I think the research community should treat this as a first-class problem, not a side note.

Two, I think the unit of contribution needs to be smaller than a full retrain. Maybe that's data, maybe it's a module or an adapter, maybe it's something like a diff that can be merged. There's been some interesting work on model merging and on weight-space editing, and I don't think any of it is mature yet, but the direction feels right. If I'm a domain expert in, say, materials science, I should have a path to improve the shared model in that area without needing ten thousand GPUs.

And three, we need the open models to actually be open in the training sense, not just the weights. The data recipes, the intermediate checkpoints, the schedule. Otherwise nobody outside can really build on them in a continual way, because you don't know where the model came from.

So the short version is, I'd like continual training to become a shared, cumulative process, rather than something each lab does behind closed doors and then ships as a new version number. That's ambitious, and there are hard problems, including how you even evaluate whether an update made the model better overall. But I think that's the direction that makes these systems genuinely useful as infrastructure, rather than products that go stale.

opus-5.5.text:
Right now continual training mostly means a lab takes its base model, collects new data, and every few months does another round of fine-tuning or a new pretraining run. It's very centralized and very episodic. The model learns in big discrete jumps, and only the people who own the weights can make it learn anything.

What I'd like to see is something closer to how people learn, where the model keeps improving from what it encounters after deployment. Today, once a model ships, it's essentially frozen. It can use context and retrieval within a session, but the weights don't absorb any of it. Every conversation, every correction a user makes, every new piece of knowledge that appears in the world is either thrown away or saved for the next big training run. That seems wasteful.

I'd also like it to be more distributed. Imagine many groups, like a hospital, a university lab, or a company with domain data, each able to contribute updates to a shared general-purpose model, instead of everyone forking their own copy and fine-tuning it in isolation. Right now we have thousands of fine-tuned variants that never talk to each other. Model merging and modular adapters hint at how you could combine those efforts, but we're far from a reliable way to let a single model keep accumulating knowledge from many sources without breaking.

That's the hard part, and why I think it's an interesting research problem rather than just an engineering one. Catastrophic forgetting is still very real. You fine-tune on one thing and quietly lose something else, often something you weren't measuring. There's also the question of trust: if many parties can update a model, how do you verify that an update is beneficial and not harmful or poisoned? And evaluation gets much harder when the model is a moving target.

So I'd like continual training to become a property of the model and the ecosystem, not a periodic ritual inside one lab. Models should keep learning safely and incrementally, from many contributors, and we should have good tools to measure what they gained and what they lost along the way. I think that would make these systems much more useful, and honestly a lot more interesting scientifically.

fable-5.text:
Thanks, Ravid, it's great to be here. So right now the situation is pretty siloed, right? Every lab takes its own base model, runs its own continual pretraining or midtraining pipeline on proprietary data, and the knowledge of how to do that well — the data mixtures, the learning rate schedules, how to avoid catastrophic forgetting — all of that stays inside the lab. What I'd really like to see is this become more of a shared, modular ecosystem.

One way to think about it is the analogy to software. When your operating system has a security issue or needs new functionality, you don't recompile the whole thing from scratch — you get a patch, an update, and there's a standard way those updates are distributed and composed. For models, we're nowhere near that. If I want a model to know about events from the last six months, or to pick up a new skill, the options are basically full retraining, which is wasteful, or ad hoc fine-tuning, which often degrades other capabilities in ways we don't measure well.

So concretely, I think three things need to develop. First, open, standardized benchmarks for continual training — not just "did the model learn the new thing," but how much did it forget, how did its calibration shift, is it still safe. Second, more research on update mechanisms that are modular and maybe even transferable across models — so an update developed on one model family could be adapted to another, rather than everyone redoing the same work. And third, honestly, more openness about the recipes themselves. Academia can contribute a lot here precisely because we're not locked into one proprietary stack — we can study continual training as a science rather than as a product pipeline. That's a big part of what motivates my group's work right now.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, I think the current situation is a bit strange if you compare it to how software evolved. In software we figured out version control, we figured out how to merge, how to send a patch upstream, how to maintain a dependency on something that keeps improving. With models we have none of that. A lab releases weights, and then a thousand groups each take those weights and go off in their own direction, and all of that work is stranded. When the next base model comes out, every one of those forks is basically thrown away and the same fine-tuning gets redone from scratch. It's an enormous amount of duplicated effort, and worse, the knowledge isn't cumulative — a great domain adaptation someone did on last year's model just doesn't transfer forward.

So what I'd want is something closer to continual training as a shared process rather than a private one. Concretely, a few things have to work that don't work yet. One is composition: if two groups each teach a model something, can I get both without the second overwriting the first? Model merging and task arithmetic are the early, honest attempts at this, and they work surprisingly often for being as crude as they are, which to me suggests there's real structure there we don't understand. Two is forgetting — continual updates degrade things nobody was measuring, and we don't have regression tests for models the way we have unit tests for code. You change a model and you genuinely don't know what you broke. Three, and this is the unglamorous one, is provenance. If a contribution turns out to be poisoned or just wrong, can you subtract it? Right now, no.

I'd also be honest that the bottleneck isn't purely technical. The groups with enough compute to run continual pretraining are the labs, and they have very little incentive to accept weight updates from outside. That's a coordination problem, not an algorithms problem.

Where I think academia fits is the science underneath — why sequential training sometimes works and sometimes collapses, how much data ordering actually matters, what the right unit of a "patch" to a model even is. You can study that at a scale where you can run many trials, and I suspect the answers will transfer up.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the ideal picture looks more like open-source software than like each lab privately fine-tuning its own copy. Right now, if a lab teaches a model something new, whether that's a skill, a domain, or fresher knowledge, that improvement stays inside its own fork. Everyone else has to repeat the work, and the effort is mostly duplicated.

What I'd like is a shared base model that many parties can keep improving over time, with their improvements being composable. Someone adds medical knowledge, someone else improves coding, someone else updates the model on recent events. Then those contributions can be combined, instead of living in separate checkpoints that can't talk to each other. There's some early evidence that this can work, for example merging models or adding small modules on top of a shared backbone. But we don't yet have a good, principled way to do it at scale.

The hard part is that continual training is fragile. When you update a model on new data, you often lose some of what it knew before, and the interactions between different updates are hard to predict. So you need a way to check that an update helps without quietly breaking something else. That makes evaluation almost as important as training. You'd want standard benchmarks and shared regression tests that any contribution has to pass before it's merged, much like continuous integration in software.

There are also practical issues, like who maintains the base model, how you handle data that can't be shared, and how you prevent bad or malicious updates. I don't think we need to solve all of that before making progress. But I do think the field would move faster if continual improvement became a collaborative, cumulative process rather than every lab starting from the same point and fine-tuning in isolation.

haiku-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think the current setup is pretty wasteful. Every lab pretrains a huge model, then does its own post-training, data curation, and continued training, and most of that work never gets shared. The same lessons get rediscovered over and over.

I think a better direction is to treat a general-purpose model as something that keeps improving over time, more like an open-source codebase than a series of disconnected releases. A few pieces would need to fit together for that to work. First, we need better ways to add new knowledge or capabilities without the model forgetting what it already knows. That's the classic continual learning problem, and it's still not really solved at scale. Second, we need modular ways to combine updates. If one group improves math reasoning and another improves multilingual ability, you should be able to merge those contributions instead of retraining from scratch. Model merging and parameter-efficient methods are early steps in that direction.

The part I find hardest is incentives and governance. Labs have strong reasons to keep their data and recipes private, and a shared model needs a way to verify contributions and catch regressions or poisoned updates. So I suspect the first version looks less like one global model and more like shared base checkpoints with community-maintained updates that are tested and versioned carefully.

I'd also push back a little on the idea that every lab has to fine-tune its own copy. Some of that is necessary because labs have different goals, but a lot of it is duplicated effort. Standardizing evaluations and data formats alone would remove a lot of waste.

So my honest answer is that the technical pieces are getting closer, but I think the real bottleneck is coordination more than algorithms.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see continual training become something that a whole community can contribute to. Right now, you can take a model and fine-tune it for your own application, but whatever it learns often stays in that particular version. It would be exciting if those improvements could feed back into a shared model that keeps getting better over time.

Different groups have different data, expertise, and computational resources. Could someone improve the model’s understanding of one scientific area, and someone else improve its ability to work in another language, and then combine those contributions? Ideally, you wouldn’t need to repeat all the earlier training.

The difficult part is making those updates work together. An improvement in one area might hurt another, so we need ways to evaluate contributions and preserve existing capabilities. But that’s the direction I’d like: learning that accumulates across both time and contributors.

Of course, with neural networks, combining those contributions is difficult. An update that helps on one task might hurt another capability. That’s the direction I’d like to see: continual training as a way to accumulate progress across the community, instead of everyone ending up with a separate branch.
